Brenda, John — thank you for having me through. I live a minute from your door, so I will be direct with you. This house needs everything: the bathrooms, the windows, the carpet, the kitchen cabinets, the garage, the electrical panel, the furnace, and a laundry room that is still sitting unfinished in a bedroom. That is not a reason to spend money before selling it. It is the reason not to. Everything that follows is the evidence, from one MLS® pull run on October 19.

2,473 square feet, a 12,195 square foot lot, and a house that needs everything.

Built in 1984. The roof was replaced about three years ago and that is the one major item behind you. Everything else is original, deferred or partly done — and we would rather put that in writing than let a buyer's inspector discover it.

What is done, and what is not

  • Done: roof approximately three years old — the single largest item a buyer discounts for
  • Partly done: air conditioning about five years, deck 2019, foyer floors, water heater 2011 and owned, some windows redone
  • Not done — the kitchen. Newer stove, fridge and countertop, but the cabinets are painted and peeling. It reads newer only against a house where nothing else has been touched
  • Not done: all three bathrooms original · windows 2000 with moisture, mould and rusted frames · carpet 1999 · garage · 100 amp original service · furnace and humidifier 2007 · no living-room lighting
  • Unfinished: the basement, and a laundry room sitting incomplete inside one of the bedrooms

This is your own house's record and it is the most useful thing in this document.

In 1991 it was listed at $299,900, failed to sell, came back $40,000 lower and sold for $250,000 — below even the reduced asking price. In 1994 it was listed again at $249,800 and expired without a sale.

Twice this house was offered at a price the market would not meet, and twice it sat. The strategy recommended in Section 10 is built to make sure that does not happen a third time.

SYNERGY's own MLS® pull, October 19, 2026: Pickering detached sales excluding Rural Pickering, grouped by the month each home was listed. October is a partial month and will fill in.

I want to be careful here, because it would be easy to tell you the market is falling and that you must act today. It is not, and you do not.

Across the Greater Toronto Area our extract holds 45,603 sales to September 30. Pickering detached in your size band ran $470 a square foot in the first quarter, $475 in the second and $469 in the third — flat across the year. In the first nineteen days of October, Pickering detached in the $700,000 to $1.3M range sold at a median of 100% of asking in 10.5 days, the firmest month of the year on both measures.

The argument for moving now is not that the market is collapsing. It is that this window is working, and that the alternative — spending months on renovations first — spends it.

One thing worth knowing that most agents will not mention. The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25%. But a buyer's budget is set by the fixed rate, and fixed rates are priced off the bond market, not off the Bank. Five-year Government of Canada yields climbed through early October and the lenders followed — BMO raised its five-year fixed 20 basis points to 5.14% on October 7.

Section 05 · Condition, basement and what they are worth

The same size house ranged from $361 to $484 a square foot this year. That spread is condition and basement.

Price per square foot is the fairest way to compare houses of similar size, and across these ten sales it ranged by a third. None of that is size. The three homes that needed work sold at $361, $384 and $398. The move-in-ready homes sold at $404 to $484.

Two honest notes. Across 171 Pickering detached sales in this size band, finished and unfinished basements show almost no difference on average — $471 against $474 a square foot. So an unfinished basement is not automatically a discount. What matters here is the specific comparison: three of the four sales closest to your size have a finished basement with a second kitchen or a separate suite. Yours is unfinished and the side entrance does not yet reach it. Against those four, that is a real gap.

The second note is the lot. At 12,195 square feet you are in the top tenth of anything selling at this size in Pickering. But across 168 sales, lot size and price per square foot correlate at only 0.15 — this market pays for the house far more than the land. The lot helps you with one particular buyer rather than with the market generally.

One more thing, because it decides whether these sales need adjusting for time. Price per square foot in this segment ran $470 in the first quarter, $475 in the second and $469 in the third — flat. The comparable sales do not need discounting to today. Note that the GTA average price rose 3.9% over the same period while price per square foot was flat: that difference is a change in what sold, not a change in what houses are worth, and it is the kind of number that sends a seller in the wrong direction.

Section 06 · The sales that decide this

The same house as yours sold in March. That is where the valuation starts.

552 and 560 Steeple Hill · Woodlands

$900,000 and $860,000

2,490 sq ft · 111 days · 75.1% of asking · vs · 6 days · 101.3% of asking

The same street, the same year, both needing work, and both with finished basements and second kitchens — which is more than you have. 552 asked $1,199,000, the price a finished house commands, and spent 111 days finding out it was not one, selling at $900,000. 560 asked $849,000, said plainly it was sold as is and required work, and was gone in six days above its asking price. This is the clearest evidence in the document, and it points at the strategy in Section 10.

1911 Rosebank Road · Amberlea

$850,000

2,138 sq ft · 7 days · 106.3% of asking · $398 per sq ft · unfinished basement

The only sale in the set that is both needs-work and unfinished-basement, which makes it the closest thing to your house that sold this year. Offered as is, no warranties, a pre-list inspection available to every buyer, contents left behind and offered separately, with a published offer date. Listed $799,900, sold $850,000 in a week. It is also 335 square feet smaller than yours, with no corner-road frontage and no hydro corridor — so it sets the rate your house should sit below, not at.

499 Lightfoot Place · Woodlands

$976,000

2,415 sq ft · 13 days · $404 per sq ft · move-in ready · finished walk-out, separate entrance, two kitchens

Within 2% of your square footage, which is why it looked like the right benchmark at first. It is not, and the difference matters. It was move-in ready, with a finished walk-out basement, its own separate entrance and two kitchens, backing onto Ernie Stroud Park at the end of a cul-de-sac. Your basement is unfinished with no entrance to it, there is no walk-out and no second kitchen, and the lot faces a road with a hydro corridor behind. $976,000 is what a finished house of this size fetches. It is the ceiling, not the comparison.

658 Cognac Crescent · Amberlea — the same house as yours

$1,025,000

2,473 sq ft · $414 per sq ft · sold March 27, 2026 · same builder layout

This is the single most useful sale in the document. The same builder layout as 700 Amaretto, in your community, the same 2,473 square feet above grade — two copies of the same house, seven months apart. Three things separate them. Their basement is partly finished with a two-piece bath and a rough-in for a shower; yours is completely unfinished with no rough-in, no bathroom and no entrance into it. Their home was in ordinary, liveable condition; yours is mostly original throughout. And they sit on an interior street on a 5,920 square foot lot, while you face the road on a corner, with a hydro corridor behind, on 12,195 square feet. $1,025,000 is the ceiling for this house — what it would fetch finished and on a quiet street. Section 07 works down from it, line by line.

692 Amaretto Avenue · four doors from you

$1,020,000

2,655 sq ft · 6 days · 107.4% of asking · $384 per sq ft · unfinished basement

You will have this number in mind, so let us meet it directly. It is 182 square feet larger, it sold in January, and it got to $1,020,000 by being listed at $949,900 and letting buyers compete — the same play recommended here. It sold in six days at 107% of asking, which tells you it showed well. At $384 a square foot it is still the lowest rate of any Amberlea sale in this size band, and that is your street's setting showing up in the numbers.

1067 Maury Crescent · Liverpool

$960,000

The one sale that backs onto a hydro field, so it is the fairest read on what the corridor costs — and it is also what your house would look like fully renovated. Updated kitchen, new broadloom, genuine pride of ownership, and it still sold at $428 a square foot while similar updated homes without a corridor reached $456 to $484, taking 33 days, the longest of any updated home here. That is the ceiling Section 10 and the renovation question measure the renovation against.

What this is built on. The strongest piece of evidence in this document is 658 Cognac Crescent — the same builder layout as your home, in your community, the same 2,473 square feet, sold seven months ago. Comparing two copies of the same house and adjusting for the differences is the most reliable method there is, and it is why the reasoning above is set out line by line rather than summarised. The condition notes came from you and from the walkthrough on October 19, and a home inspection could move this either way — which is why we pay for one before the house goes up.

This is a lower number than any seller wants to hear, and I would rather give it to you now than have you discover it in week six. It is lower because 658 Cognac had a basement you could use and a house you could move into, and because your lot faces a road with a corridor behind it. What you have that they did not is more than double the land. The strategy in Section 10 is built to get you above this number, not to settle at it.

It also sets the ceiling honestly. The move-in-ready homes are asking $1,095,000 to $1,100,000, and the one out longest, at $1.1M, has sat 59 days and already cut its price.

Section 09 · Who buys a home like yours

Two buyers, and both of them are shopping for exactly what you have.

This is not guesswork. The gap between a needs-work home and a finished one in this size band is $136,000 to $198,000. That gap is a renovator's margin — it is the reason this buyer exists, and the reason they move quickly when something like yours appears.

The contractor or investor

They price the work rather than fear it. A 100 amp service, a 2007 furnace and 1999 carpet are line items to them, not deal-breakers — and the roof already being done is the thing that makes the file work. The side entrance from the garage, with room to create a walk-up, is the detail that decides it: four of the ten comparable sales had a second kitchen or a walkout, and yours has the space to add one. With nine active listings in this size band and not one of them a project, they currently have nowhere else to go.

The family renovating to stay

Usually trading up from a smaller Amberlea or Rougemount home, often with parents to accommodate. They want the school catchment, a real lot and a layout they can change — and at 12,195 square feet on a corner, your lot is in the top tenth of anything selling at this size. They will take four bedrooms, 2,473 square feet and a kitchen from 2014 and make the rest theirs over a few years.

Who will not buy it, and why that is fine

The buyer who wants to move in and change nothing. They are being served right now by 1905 Wildflower and 1446 Sandhurst at $1,095,000 and up. Marketing to them wastes the weeks that matter, and it is how a house ends up where 552 Steeple Hill ended up. We will not chase them.

About the clear-out. You have told us there is a great deal to move. That is the single most common reason a sale gets delayed by months, and it is the part people dread. We rent the bin, put it on the driveway, and bring a crew to empty the house once you have taken out everything you want to keep. Then a professional clean, then photography. You do not lift anything and you do not pay for any of it separately — a $3,000 to $4,000 value that sits inside the fee.

Rates shown are total commission including the co-operating brokerage's share, plus HST. Commission is negotiable.

Questions sellers ask

The things worth asking, answered before you have to ask them.

Why not renovate first, the way we have been advised?

Because of what the work costs against what it returns. You have put the job at $160,000 at minimum and $180,000 on average. The one comparable sale that is both fully updated and backs a hydro corridor — 1067 Maury — sold at $428 a square foot, which puts a fully finished 700 Amaretto at about $1,058,000. Spend $180,000 and carry the house four more months and you are at roughly $874,000, about $59,000 ahead of selling now — and only if the work goes perfectly and achieves that finished price. 1067 Maury was in exactly that condition and still took 33 days at 96.1% of asking. If the work lands short of a full finish, which $180,000 very likely does in a house with original paint and wallpaper throughout, you end up between $756,000 and $793,000 — $22,000 to $59,000 behind where you are today.

What is wrong with doing part of it?

A half-renovated house is the worst of both. The contractor who would have paid for the opportunity no longer sees one, and the buyer who wants to move in still sees work. That is exactly what 552 Steeple Hill was — a home that needed work, asking the price of a finished one. It took 111 days and sold for a quarter below its asking price.

Why list at $799,000?

Because it is what the evidence supports, and publishing it openly is what creates competition. The same builder layout as your home — 658 Cognac Crescent — sold for $1,025,000 in March with a partly finished basement, in liveable condition, on an interior street. Working down from that for your unfinished basement, the condition of the house and the corner-and-corridor setting gives $790,000 to $845,000. Listing at $799,000 with a published offer date brings several buyers through on the same weekend. Three homes nearby did exactly this in 2026 and all three sold above their asking price within a week; applying what they achieved gives $809,000 to $858,000. You are never obliged to accept an offer, whatever the list price says.

What if only one buyer turns up on the offer date?

Then you do not have to accept the offer. An offer date is a date for reviewing offers, not a commitment to sell. If the response is thin we talk it through and adjust, and you are better off knowing that in week one than in month three.

Has this house struggled to sell before?

Twice. In 1991 it was listed at $299,900, terminated without selling, came back at $259,900 and sold for $250,000. In 1994 it was listed at $249,800 and expired unsold. Both times the asking price was ahead of what the market would pay, and both times the house sat. That is the single best reason to price this one to bring buyers in rather than to hope.

Does the unfinished basement hurt us?

Against the specific homes you are competing with, yes. Three of the four sales closest to your square footage have a finished basement with a second kitchen or a separate suite, and you have an unfinished basement with no entrance into it. Across the wider market it matters less than you might think — 171 Pickering sales in your size band show almost no difference between finished and unfinished. But buyers compare you to the four, not to the 171. The honest answer is that the side entrance from the garage gives a buyer room to create a walk-up, and that possibility is worth more to the right buyer than a finished rec room would be.

Does the hydro corridor hurt us?

It costs something and we have measured it rather than guessed. The one comparable sale backing a hydro field sold at $428 a square foot while similar updated homes without one reached $456 to $484, and it took the longest to sell of any updated home in the set. That is roughly $28 to $56 a square foot, and it is already inside the valuation. A buyer's agent will raise it; better that we raise it first, with a number attached.

Will the 100 amp service and the 2007 furnace scare buyers off?

Not the buyer we are marketing to, and not if we disclose them properly. A contractor prices a panel upgrade and a furnace without blinking. What frightens buyers is finding things out late — which is why we pay for a home inspection before the house goes up and hand it to every buyer. It takes away the excuse to bid low on uncertainty, and it is included in the fee.

Will I owe tax on the sale?

For a home you have lived in, the principal-residence exemption generally covers the gain. It is the exceptions that cost people money — years the home was rented, a basement suite, land over half a hectare, a period of non-residency. Ask us and we will walk your ownership history year by year. We flag; we do not guess.

Who actually clears the house?

We do. We rent the bin, put it on your driveway and bring a crew in once you have taken out everything you want to keep. Then a professional clean. You do not lift anything and it is not billed to you — it sits inside the fee and is worth $3,000 to $4,000.

How quickly could this happen?

Five to seven days from the bin arriving to the listing going live, then a week on the market to the offer date. Homes listed in Pickering this September and October have been selling in eleven days.

Who will I actually be dealing with?

Terrence, throughout. I live a minute away, I will run this listing personally, and you will hear from me at every stage — not only when there is news.

From here to sold

A conversation first, then a week of work.

Nothing here commits you to anything. Read it, disagree with it, and let us talk it through together.

Step one · read it overTake your time with this, both of you. Mark anything you disagree with — particularly the condition notes and the valuation. If something in here is wrong, I would rather know now.
Step two · we talk it throughHalf an hour, at your kitchen table or on the phone. We go through the numbers, the strategy and anything you want a second look at — including whether selling is the right move at all. If the answer is to stay, that is a perfectly good answer.
Step three · you decide what you are keepingWalk the house and set aside what is coming with you. Everything else we handle.
Step four · the weekBin and crew, professional clean, inspection, photography, video and drone, floor plans. Live on MLS® in five to seven days.
Step five · the offer dateOpen houses both weekend days, offers reviewed on a published date, and you choose — or you do not. Either way you will hear from me throughout, not just when there is news.

From the day you say go, roughly two weeks to offers in hand.

When you're ready

Read it over, then let's talk it through.

There is no decision to make today, and take as long as you need with it. When you are ready, I am a minute away. If you believe a sale is in your best interest we are glad to explore it together — and if the answer is to hold, that is a perfectly good answer too.
